course_title: Programming for Everybody (Getting Started with Python)
chapter_title: Installing Python and Writing Your First Program
chapter_summary:
Before you can write programs, you need Python installed on your computer. Python is free, open-source software that runs on every major operating system. The installation process is straightforward and takes only a few minutes.

**Installing Python on Windows:**
1. Visit https://www.python.org/downloads/ and download the latest Python 3 installer for Windows.
2. Run the installer. **Important:** Check the box that says "Add Python to PATH" before clicking Install. This allows you to run Python from the command prompt.
3. After installation, open Command Prompt and type `python --version` to verify the installation.

**Installing Python on macOS:**
1. macOS comes with Python 2 pre-installed, but you need Python 3. Visit https://www.python.org/downloads/ and download the macOS installer.
2. Run the installer and follow the prompts.
3. Open Terminal and type `python3 --version` to verify.

**Installing Python on Linux:**
1. Most Linux distributions come with Python 3 pre-installed. Open a terminal and type `python3 --version` to check.
2. If it is not installed, use your package manager: `sudo apt-get install python3` (Ubuntu/Debian) or `sudo dnf install python3` (Fedora).

**The Python interpreter:**

Once Python is installed, you can open the **interactive interpreter** by typing `python` (Windows) or `python3` (macOS/Linux) in your terminal/command prompt. You will see a prompt that looks like `>>>`. This means Python is waiting for you to type a command. You can type any Python expression and see the result immediately.

```python
>>> 2 + 3
5
>>> print("Hello!")
Hello!
>>> name = "Alice"
>>> print(name)
Alice
```

The interactive interpreter is excellent for experimenting and learning. You can test ideas, explore how functions work, and debug small pieces of code. However, when you write a real program, you write it in a **script file** — a text file with a `.py` extension — and run the entire file at once.

**Writing a script:**

1. Open a text editor. You can use VS Code, Notepad (Windows), TextEdit (macOS), or any plain text editor. Do not use Microsoft Word or Google Docs — these are word processors, not text editors, and they add invisible formatting that breaks code.
2. Type the following program:
   ```python
   # myfirstprogram.py
   print("Hello, world!")
   print("I am learning Python.")
   name = "Alice"
   print("My name is", name)
   ```
3. Save the file as `myfirstprogram.py` in a folder you can find easily.
4. Open your terminal/command prompt, navigate to the folder, and run:
   ```bash
   python myfirstprogram.py
   ```
   (On macOS/Linux, use `python3 myfirstprogram.py`)

**Interactive mode vs. script mode:**

- **Interactive mode:** You type one line at a time and see the result immediately. Good for experiments and quick calculations. Bad for writing complex programs because your work is lost when you close the interpreter.
- **Script mode:** You write your program in a file and run the entire file. Good for real programs that you want to save, edit, and run repeatedly. The file is your permanent record.

Think of interactive mode as a scratchpad and script mode as writing a letter. You use the scratchpad for quick notes and the letter for formal communication.

**The Python Playground:**

If you cannot install Python on your computer, you can use the **Python Playground** — an online environment where you can write and run Python code in your browser. This is useful for learners who are using shared computers, Chromebooks, or devices where installation is restricted. The Playground is not a replacement for a local Python installation, but it is a great tool for getting started.

**Common installation mistakes:**
- Not checking "Add Python to PATH" on Windows. This means the command prompt cannot find Python.
- Using Python 2 instead of Python 3. Python 2 is obsolete.
- Saving the file with a `.txt` extension instead of `.py`. The file must end with `.py` for Python to recognize it as a program.
- Using a word processor instead of a text editor. Word processors add hidden formatting characters.

screens.title: Installing Python and Writing Your First Program
screens.subtitle: Set up Python 3, run the interpreter, and create your first .py script

narration.text: In this chapter you will set up a working Python environment and run your first small program. We focus on practical, step-by-step tasks: downloading and installing Python three on Windows, Mac O S or Linux; opening the interactive interpreter to try quick expressions; and writing a saved script file that you can run again and again. You’ll also learn typical errors to watch for, how to verify your installation, and what to do if you cannot install locally by using an online playground. For example, you will run the print function, create a variable that holds a name, and save a file called myfirstprogram dot P Y file that prints a few lines. This matters because without a correct installation and the right file format you can’t run programs or learn effectively. By the end of this chapter you will be able to confirm Python is installed, run quick experiments in the interpreter, and write and run a reusable script. Think about where you will save your first dot P Y file file and whether you prefer experimenting in the interpreter or writing a script you can edit later.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you will be able to demonstrate after this chapter

narration.text: These four objectives describe the practical skills you will carry forward. First, you will install Python three on Windows, Mac O S, or Linux and confirm the installation with a version check. This is fundamental because your terminal must locate the Python executable for programs to run. Second, you will open and use the interactive interpreter to try expressions, call the print function, and inspect variables. The interpreter is your quick feedback loop for testing ideas. Third, you will write, save, and run a Python script file with a dot P Y file extension. Saving programs as files is how you build work that lasts. Fourth, you will understand the difference between interactive mode and script mode so you can choose the right workflow: interactive for exploration, script files for programs you want to store and run repeatedly. Each objective includes a short reason and a concrete example so you can practice with confidence.

narration.text: Now we make each objective concrete so you can practice and verify your work. To demonstrate installation, run the appropriate version command — on Windows use python --version and on Mac O S or Linux use Python three --version — and show the expected Python three output. To show you can use the interpreter, open it, type a simple arithmetic expression and the print function with a string, and observe immediate results. To prove you can write and run a script, create a file named myfirstprogram dot P Y file that prints several lines, save it as plain text, and run it from the terminal. screens.title: Install Python 3: overview and preparation
screens.subtitle: Decide which installer or package to use and prepare your terminal

narration.text: Installing Python starts with a small checklist and a correct installer. First, choose Python three, not Python 2, since Python 2 is obsolete. On all systems you can get the official installers; the main choices are an installer for Windows and Mac O S or the system package manager on Linux. Before installing on Windows, prepare by checking the installer option to add Python to PATH so the command prompt will find it. On Mac O S and Linux, be ready to use Python three on the terminal if the default python points to an older version. A good preparation step is to plan where to save your scripts so you can navigate to that folder in a terminal. This prevents confusion when you run a script from a different directory. A common misconception is that installation always sets up terminal access automatically; on Windows the PATH box is easy to miss. A quick test after installation is to run the version command for your OS. That confirmation tells you the installation succeeded and the terminal can reach Python. Think about your preferred editor so you are ready to create dot P Y file files next.

keyIdea.text: Choose Python 3, enable PATH on Windows, know your version command, and pick a folder for scripts.

screens.title: Windows installation steps
screens.subtitle: Download the installer, enable PATH, and verify with a version check

narration.text: Installing Python on Windows is a short, guided process but it has a key checkbox that learners often miss. First, download the latest Python three installer. When you run it, look for and check the Add Python to PATH box before you press Install. This small action makes the python command available from Command Prompt without additional setup. After installation completes, open Command Prompt and type python --version to verify that Command Prompt can find the interpreter and that it is Python three. If the command fails, you either need to re-run the installer and enable the PATH option, or add Python to PATH manually using system environment settings. Another common mistake is saving a program with a. txt extension because Notepad may default to that; always choose Save As and select All Files then type the dot P Y file extension explicitly. As a concrete example, create a folder named python-sandbox, save myfirstprogram dot P Y file inside it, open Command Prompt, navigate to that folder, and run python myfirstprogram dot P Y file to see the program output.

keyIdea.title: Windows tip
keyIdea.text: Always check Add Python to PATH during installation and verify with python --version in Command Prompt.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Windows Install
Windows installation steps
A clear sequence to make Python available from the Command Prompt.
  1. Download the latest Python 3 installer for Windows.
  2. Run the installer and check Add Python to PATH.
  3. Choose Install Now and complete the setup.

screens.title: macOS installation and verification
screens.subtitle: Get Python 3 and confirm with python3 in Terminal

narration.text: On Mac O S the system may include an older Python 2, so you need to install Python three and use the Python three command in Terminal. Choose the Mac O S installer for Python three, run the package and follow the prompts. After installation, open Terminal and type Python three --version. If it reports a Python three version, you’re ready to use the interpreter. A typical confusion is trying plain python at the Mac O S terminal and getting the older version; using Python three avoids that. For practice, open Terminal, run Python three to enter interactive mode, then try a basic calculation and use the print function with a small string. When you exit the interpreter, use the exit command or control-D. Keep in mind that saving files and running scripts will use Python three myscript dot P Y file when you invoke them from Terminal. This ensures your commands run with the correct runtime. The Mac O S workflow is reliable once you adopt the Python three convention and verify the version. macOS installation and verification means use the python3 command to avoid the system python 2 and confirm installation with python3 --version.. In practical terms, get python 3 and confirm with python3 in terminal. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.subtitle: Check for preinstalled Python 3 and install via package manager if needed

narration.text: Many Linux distributions include Python three already. Start by opening a terminal and running Python three --version. If Python three is present you can proceed to using the interpreter or creating scripts. If not installed, use the distribution package manager. For Debian and Ubuntu, the command sudo apt-get install Python three installs Python three. On Fedora, use sudo dnf install Python three. After installing, repeat the version check. A helpful practice is creating a small folder for your scripts and using the terminal to change into it before running files. A common mistaken expectation is that package managers and installers leave the same command names across distributions; remember to use Python three for running the interpreter and scripts. Also be mindful of permissions when installing system packages: sudo elevates privileges on Debian-based and Fedora systems. Once installed, you can test the interpreter immediately with simple expressions. This approach keeps your environment consistent with command-line workflows used in classroom exercises. Linux installation and using package managers means use your distro's package manager to install python3 when needed and confirm with python3 --version.. In practical terms, check for preinstalled python 3 and install via package manager if needed. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Using the interactive interpreter
screens.subtitle: Try expressions, set variables, and call the print function

narration.text: The interactive interpreter is a scratchpad where you can type one expression or statement at a time and immediately see results. You open it by running python on Windows or Python three on Mac O S and Linux. At the prompt you will see >>> and you can type an arithmetic expression like two plus three and see five returned immediately. You can also assign variables and call the print function to send output to the screen. For example, assign a name variable and then call the print function to display it; this is ideal for testing short code fragments and debugging ideas. A misconception is that interactive mode saves your work — it does not. When you close the interpreter the history is lost unless you use features like readline history, so interactive mode is best for quick experiments, not permanent programs. Try the interpreter for immediate feedback, then move tested code into a dot P Y file file when you want to keep it. Using the interactive interpreter means use the interpreter for experimentation and immediate feedback; it does not save your session as a script does.. In practical terms, try expressions, set variables, and call the print function. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Interpreter role

screens.title: Writing your first Python script
screens.subtitle: Create a plain text file named myfirstprogram.py and save simple print statements

narration.text: Writing a Python script means placing your program text into a plain text file with a dot P Y file extension. Use a simple editor like V S Code, Notepad on Windows, or TextEdit set to plain text on Mac O S. Do not use a word processor because it adds invisible formatting that causes syntax errors. Type a few print statements and an assignment, then save the file as myfirstprogram dot P Y file in a folder you can find easily. For example, your file might include a line that prints Hello, world!, another that prints I am learning Python, and a variable assignment that prints your name. The file is your permanent record of the program and can be edited and rerun. A common mistake is saving the file as myfirstprogram. txt; the dot P Y file extension must be explicitly chosen. When you save and navigate to the folder in a terminal, you will run the script with the python or Python three command depending on your system. This workflow turns experiments into repeatable programs. Writing your first Python script means use a plain text editor and save code in a .py file so python recognizes and runs it.. In practical terms, create a plain text file named myfirstprogram.py and save simple print statements. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Write a Script
Writing your first Python script
Create myfirstprogram.py using a plain text editor and include several print statements.
Editor guidance
  • Use a plain text editor: VS Code, Notepad, or TextEdit in plain text mode.
  • Do not use a word processor like Word or Google Docs.
  • Save the file with a .py extension explicitly.
Example file: myfirstprogram.py
# myfirstprogram.py
print("Hello, world!")
print("I am learning Python.")

Practical note
Save in a known folder and open a terminal there to run the script reliably.

screens.title: Running a script from the terminal
screens.subtitle: Navigate to the folder and run python or python3 with the script filename

narration.text: Running a saved Python script uses a simple terminal workflow. First, open your Command Prompt or Terminal and change directory to the folder where you saved your dot P Y file file. On Windows, use the cd command to reach the folder. On Mac O S and Linux, use cd similarly. Once you are in the right folder, run the script with python myfirstprogram dot P Y file on Windows or Python three myfirstprogram dot P Y file on Mac O S and Linux, depending on how Python is installed. The terminal will execute the file top to bottom and show the printed output. A common error is running the command from the wrong directory which results in a file-not-found message; navigate to the correct folder or pass a full path to the file. Another pitfall is using a. txt extension by accident; ensure the file ends with dot P Y file. As an example, saving myfirstprogram dot P Y file with several print statements and then running the appropriate command should produce the printed lines in your terminal. This workflow turns your saved code into repeatable programs.

keyIdea.title: Run command
keyIdea.text: Navigate to your script's folder and run python myfirstprogram.py or python3 myfirstprogram.py as appropriate.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Run a Script
Running a script from the terminal
Change to the script folder then execute the file with the system Python command.
Steps to run
  1. Open Command Prompt or Terminal and change directory to your script folder.
  2. Run: python myfirstprogram.py on Windows, or python3 myfirstprogram.py on macOS/Linux.
  3. Observe printed output displayed in the terminal.
Terminal example
C:\Users\You> cd python-sandbox
C:\Users\You\python-sandbox> python myfirstprogram.py

I am learning Python.
My name is Alice

# macOS / Linux
$ cd ~/python-sandbox
$ python3 myfirstprogram.py
Common mistake
Running from the wrong directory causes file-not-found errors. Use cd to enter the script folder first.

screens.title: Interactive mode vs. script mode
screens.subtitle: When to use the interpreter and when to write a .py file

narration.text: Interactive mode and script mode serve different purposes. Interactive mode is a temporary scratchpad: you type one line or expression and immediately see results. It is ideal for experimentation, quick calculations, and learning how a function behaves. For example, you can call the print function or compute a calculation and immediately inspect the value of a variable. Script mode uses a saved dot P Y file file that you run as a complete program; it is best for building programs you want to keep, edit, and run repeatedly. A common learner error is relying solely on the interpreter and not saving important work. Another confusion is thinking that script mode is harder — starting with a short script of a few print statements is an easy step forward. Use interactive mode to test ideas and script mode to preserve and share finished work. As a practical exercise, try the same simple program in both modes: type the lines into the interpreter, then save them in a file and run the file to compare behaviors and convenience. Interactive mode vs. script mode means use the interpreter for fast feedback and scripts for saved, repeatable programs you edit and run later.. In practical terms, when to use the interpreter and when to write a .py file. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Interactive vs Script
Interactive mode vs. script mode
Interactive mode
Type single expressions or statements and see immediate results at the prompt.
  • Best for experiments and debugging.
  • Immediate feedback but not saved by default.
  • Use python or python3 to open the prompt.
Script mode
Write a .py file, save it, and run the whole file at once from the terminal.
  • Best for programs you want to keep and reuse.
  • Allows editing, versioning, and sharing as files.
  • Run with python myfile.py or python3 myfile.py.
Try this
Type three lines in the interpreter and then save and run the same three lines in a .py file to compare behaviors and persistence.

screens.title: Common installation mistakes and the Python Playground
screens.subtitle: Fix PATH issues, extension mistakes, and use an online alternative when needed

narration.text: Several common problems block learners during setup, but each has a simple fix. On Windows, forgetting to check Add Python to PATH prevents the terminal from finding the interpreter; the remedy is to rerun the installer with that option selected or add Python to PATH manually. Another frequent error is saving code with a. txt extension or using a word processor that inserts hidden formatting; always use a plain text editor and the dot P Y file extension. Using Python 2 by mistake can occur on older systems; check the version command and prefer Python three. If installation is impossible because of permissions or a locked-down device, use an online Python Playground where you can write and run code in your browser. The Playground is a safe alternative for practice, but it is not a full replacement for a local installation because it does not teach environment setup. For each problem, try a small verification step: run the version command and run a one-line print program to confirm that the fix worked. This approach helps you move past common roadblocks quickly.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshooting
keyIdea.text: Address PATH errors, file extension mistakes, and know the Playground as a browser-based alternative for practice.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Troubleshooting
Common installation mistakes and the Python Playground
PATH not set
If the terminal reports Python is not recognized, rerun the installer and check Add Python to PATH or update environment variables manually.
Wrong extension
Saving files as .txt prevents Python from recognizing them. Use Save As and type .py explicitly when saving.
Word processor formatting
Word processors add invisible characters that break code. Use plain text editors only.
Python 2 vs 3
If python invokes Python 2, use python3 to run Python 3, or update PATH to prefer Python 3.
Python Playground
Use the browser-based Playground when you cannot install locally. It replicates the interpreter for learning purposes, but it does not replace learning how to install and run local scripts.
Quick checks
After fixes, run the version command and a one-line print program to confirm success.
Hands-on reminder
If you cannot install Python, complete the exercises using the Playground and then repeat them locally when you have installation access.

narration.text: Here are the key concepts to remember from this chapter. First, install Python three and verify it with the appropriate version command; on Windows use python --version and on Mac O S and Linux use Python three --version when needed. Second, the interactive interpreter is a quick way to test expressions and call the print function, but its work is temporary unless you save it. Third, scripts are plain text files with a dot P Y file extension that you save, edit, and run from the terminal for repeatable programs. Keep these concepts together as part of your setup workflow: confirm installation, try quick ideas in the interpreter, then save working code in a dot P Y file file and run it from the terminal. These steps will let you move from experimentation to building programs you can keep and improve over time.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Quick reference
Verify version
Run the appropriate version command and confirm Python 3 is accessible from the terminal.
Use .py files
Save code in plain text with a .py extension so Python runs it correctly.
Interpreter vs Script
Use the interpreter for experiments and scripts when you want to save and run programs again.
Key Takeaway

Follow these simple checks to avoid common pitfalls and make your first programs run smoothly.
